chunks: My father narrated, may God be pleased with him, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to me, saying: Sahl ibn Ziyad al-Adamy narrated to me, saying: Al-Hasan ibn al-Hussein al-Lu'lu'i narrated to me, from Muhammad ibn Sinan, from Zayd Abu Usamah al-Shaham, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said: The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said:

Indeed, a great calamity is rewarded with a great recompense. And when God loves a servant, He tests him with a great calamity. So whoever is pleased with it, for him is God's pleasure. And whoever is displeased with the calamity, for him is God's displeasure.
ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual significance of suffering in Shia theology according to the hadith of al-Khisal?
ai.summary: In al-Khisal, Shaykh al-Saduq presents this hadith as a cornerstone of Shia theodicy, framing severe trials not as punishment but as a distinct sign of divine intimacy and love. The narration emphasizes that the magnitude of the reward is directly proportional to the magnitude of the calamity, contingent upon the servant's internal state of acceptance (riḍā) versus discontent (sukhṭ). This concept aligns with the Shia understanding of the Imams' own sufferings as exemplary models of enduring hardship with grace to attain high spiritual ranks.

en.dr-ali-peiravi: 1-64 (The compiler of the book narrated) that his father - may God be pleased with him - narrated that Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar quoted on the authority of Sahl ibn Zyad al-Adamy, on the authority of Al-Hassan ibn al-Hussein al-Lu’lu’ee, on the authority of Muhammad ibn Sin’an, on the authority of Zayd Abi Usamah ash-Shaham, on the authority of Aba Abdullah as-Sadiq (MGB) that God’s Prophet (MGB) said,

“There is a great reward for a great calamity. If he is pleased with the calamity, then God the Honorable the Exalted will be pleased with him. However, if he is displeased with the calamity, then God will be displeased with him.”
